subject: pathology
title: Mendelian Inheritance Patterns, Genetic Penetrance, and Autosomal Dominance

steps.tx: Monogenic diseases caused by single-gene mutations adhere to predictable transmission probabilities governed by principles of segregating alleles. Understanding these classic transmission modes constitutes the study of clinical **Mendelian inheritance**, encompassing autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and sex-linked patterns that determine disease recurrence in subsequent family generations.
steps.say: Mendelian inheritance describes single-gene disorders transmitting along predictable family pedigrees.

nodes.label: Pathogenic Point Mutation in a Single Nuclear Gene
Meiotic Segregation of Maternal and Paternal Alleles
Predictable Transmission Ratios Manifest Across Generations

steps.tx: In single-gene disorders displaying dominant expression, inheritance of a single mutant allele from either parent is sufficient to produce clinical disease. Because every affected individual possesses one mutant and one normal allele, each offspring carries a fifty percent recurrence risk under **autosomal dominant inheritance**, exemplified by adult polycystic kidney disease.
steps.say: Autosomal dominant disorders require only one mutant allele and show vertical pedigree transmission.

vis.alt: Autosomal dominant inheritance shown as a vertical pedigree from one mutant allele
vis.caption: Autosomal dominant inheritance needs only one mutant allele, and the disorder passes down a vertical pedigree. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Disorders manifesting only when both maternal and paternal alleles at a given locus carry loss-of-function mutations follow recessive inheritance. Unaffected heterozygous parents act as carriers, conferring a twenty-five percent risk of homozygous disease among their offspring under **autosomal recessive inheritance**.
steps.say: Autosomal recessive diseases require two mutant alleles and typically involve metabolic enzyme defects.

left.title: Dominant Structural Defects
points: Mutations encode altered structural proteins or receptor subunits
Exert dominant-negative interference on macromolecular multimeric complexes
Show vertical pedigree transmission through successive generations
Often present in late childhood or adulthood with variable clinical expressivity

right.title: Recessive Enzyme Deficiencies
points: Loss-of-function mutations affecting catalytic cellular enzymes
Half-normal enzyme activity in heterozygotes maintains physiological homeostasis
Show horizontal pedigree distribution confined to sibships of carrier parents
Typically present early in infancy with uniform, severe metabolic derangement

steps.tx: Sex-linked transmission occurs when disease-causing mutant alleles reside upon the X chromosome. Because biological males carry a single X chromosome, hemizygous males express the disease phenotype, while heterozygous females remain asymptomatic carriers, illustrating classic **X-linked recessive inheritance**, which lacks direct father-to-son transmission across family pedigrees.
steps.say: X-linked recessive disorders express fully in hemizygous males, with no direct father-to-son transmission.

steps.tx: The prototypic autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by heterozygous mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15q21 is **Marfan syndrome**. This disease impairs microfibrillar scaffolding of elastic fibers, producing prominent pleiotropic pathology across skeletal, cardiovascular, and ocular systems throughout the patient's lifetime.
steps.say: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant fibrillin-1 disorder affecting skeleton, eyes, and aorta.

vis.alt: Marfan syndrome with long limbs, upward lens dislocation and aortic root dilatation
vis.caption: Marfan syndrome is shown across the skeleton, the upward dislocation of the lens, and the widened aortic root. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Skeletal manifestations of Marfan syndrome stem from excessive, unconstrained linear bone growth. Affected patients exhibit unusually tall stature, abnormally long slender extremities, an increased arm-span-to-height ratio, joint laxity, pectus excavatum, and arachnodactyly, a distinctive constellation of clinical signs designated as **dolichostenomelia**.
steps.say: Dolichostenomelia describes the tall stature, long limbs, and spider fingers seen in Marfan patients.

nodes.label: Mutant Fibrillin Fails to Regulate Periosteal Growth Factors

steps.tx: Cardiovascular pathology represents the most lethal complication in patients with Marfan syndrome. Fragmentation of elastic laminae in the aortic tunica media produces cystic medial degeneration, causing ascending aortic root aneurysm that predisposes to life-threatening **aortic dissection in Marfan**, requiring elective root replacement.
steps.say: Cystic medial necrosis of the ascending aorta predisposes Marfan patients to fatal aortic dissection.

nodes.label: Fragmentation of Elastic Laminae in Aortic Tunica Media
Accumulation of Basophilic Ground Substance in Media
Progressive Annuloaortic Ectasia and Valve Regurgitation
Catastrophic Intimal Tear and False Lumen Aortic Dissection

steps.tx: Ocular manifestations in Marfan syndrome result from structural laxity of ciliary zonules that suspend the crystalline lens. Bilateral dislocation, typically displaced in an upward and outward direction, represents the diagnostic hallmark termed **ectopia lentis**, contrasting sharply with downward dislocation seen in homocystinuria.
steps.say: Ectopia lentis in Marfan syndrome presents with upward and temporal dislocation of the lens.
